findings.description: Attributes anticipatory intent to 1966 drafters: 'a design choice that anticipates the psychological dimension of economic and social disruption.' The historical record indicates the drafters included mental health because of the WHO constitutional definition of health (1946) and post-war psychiatric awareness — not because they foresaw AI-driven economic disruption. The claim conflates the provision's current applicability with the drafters' documented legislative intent.
findings.suggestion: Replace with language distinguishing scope from intent: 'a design choice whose scope reaches the psychological dimension of economic and social disruption' or 'the inclusion of mental health — reflecting the WHO's 1946 definition — means the article's scope extends to the psychological dimension of economic disruption.'
findings.context: The article covers both physical and mental health — a design choice that anticipates the psychological dimension of economic and social disruption.

findings.description: Acemoglu & Restrepo (2020) cited alongside McKinsey and Goldman Sachs without noting its substantively different conclusion. McKinsey/Goldman project large displacement potential; Acemoglu & Restrepo demonstrate that automation displacement gets partially offset by new task creation, yielding more modest net effects. Citing all three under a single 'Research suggests' framing conflates divergent estimates and obscures the scholarly debate about net vs. gross displacement.
findings.suggestion: Either separate the citations by conclusion direction ('some analyses project substantial displacement [McKinsey, Goldman], while others find displacement partially offset by new task creation [Acemoglu & Restrepo, 2020]') or drop Acemoglu & Restrepo from this particular claim and cite it where discussing offsetting effects.
findings.context: Research suggests AI automation could affect a substantial share of current work activities within a decade (McKinsey Global Institute, 2023; Goldman Sachs, 2023; Acemoglu & Restrepo, 2020)

findings.description: Claims 'Analysts have applied the protocol seven times across the project' with a specific enumeration (H1-H7, R1-R7, LA1-LA5, technology stack, landing page strategy, quality floor analysis, PSQ-UDHR evaluation) but no hyperlinks or page references to verify each application. The parenthetical counts to more than seven distinct applications. For a researcher-facing page, verifiable cross-references would strengthen the claim.
findings.suggestion: Either link each application to its documentation page, or replace the specific count with a general claim ('applied across multiple analytical domains') if exact enumeration proves unwieldy.
findings.context: Analysts have applied the protocol seven times across the project (H1–H7 hypotheses, R1–R7 counterfactuals, LA1–LA5 litigation mechanisms, technology stack, landing page strategy, quality floor analysis, and PSQ-UDHR evaluation).

findings.description: States 'Current U.S. policy does not have a comprehensive AI transition framework' as unqualified fact. The CHIPS and Science Act (2022), Executive Order 14110 on AI (October 2023), NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and various state-level AI governance initiatives constitute partial policy responses. The claim may hold under a strict definition of 'comprehensive' but presents as a binary absence rather than a gap relative to the Article 2 standard. Fair witness discipline calls for specifying the threshold that 'comprehensive' implies.
findings.suggestion: Qualify the threshold: 'Current U.S. policy lacks a comprehensive workforce transition framework proportional to projected AI displacement scale' or 'No unified federal AI transition framework exists, though partial measures (workforce retraining programs, NIST frameworks, executive orders) address specific dimensions.'
findings.context: Current U.S. policy does not have a comprehensive AI transition framework.

findings.description: Claims a theoretical framework represents 'the hardest thing to establish' for a new discipline — an evaluative assertion presented as observation. Establishing journals, conferences, and citation networks requires institutional coordination, funding, and community formation that arguably exceeds the difficulty of writing a theoretical document. The claim privileges the author's contribution without evidence for the comparative difficulty ranking.
findings.suggestion: Replace the evaluative ranking with a descriptive claim: 'But it has something necessary for a discipline to form: a theoretical framework grounded in existing science...' This preserves the argument without the unsupported difficulty hierarchy.
findings.context: The discipline does not yet have a journal, a conference, or an established citation network. But it has the hardest thing to establish: a theoretical framework grounded in existing science

epistemic_flags: Scan covers a large delta (90+ commits, 16 content files); focused reading on 7 most substantive recent files. Findings biased toward articles read in full.
Acemoglu & Restrepo characterization (f2) based on knowledge-base understanding of the 2020 paper; verify against the specific claims made in their abstract before acting on this finding.
Article 2 policy vacuum claim (f4) sensitivity depends on temporal scope — EO 14110 status may have changed post-January 2026 given the political context described in the sixtieth-anniversary post.
